overview: Nobatia, also called Nobadia, was a kingdom of Lower Nubia. Houses, royal burials and churches reveal different settings of life. Its later union with Makuria changed political institutions while regional communities and crafts continued.

periods.title: Royal power and river communities
periods.summary: Large tombs at Ballana and Qustul display elite wealth and connections beyond Nubia. Greek records name Noubadia. These are traces of developing royal power, not a complete picture of ordinary households.

periods.title: Christian institutions emerge
periods.summary: Nobatian rulers adopted Christianity around the mid-sixth century. A royal conversion date does not establish when every inhabitant changed religious practice.

periods.title: Church building and political change
periods.summary: Faras’s early seventh-century church documents Christian institutions. The chronology of Nobatia’s union with Makuria remains disputed.

periods.title: Faras within a continuing Nubian world
periods.summary: Faras developed a cathedral and a long tradition of painted interiors after the period of independent Nobatian kingship. The surviving art belongs to successive generations.

periods.title: After the medieval kingdoms
periods.summary: The wider Nubian state fragmented after prolonged internal conflict and interference from Egypt. Political institutions changed; the medieval remains became evidence for later generations studying the region.

periods.title: Rescuing and studying the evidence
periods.summary: Archaeological rescue work at Faras recovered painted plaster, inscriptions and other objects before flooding associated with the Aswan High Dam. Preserved objects allow new study of medieval life.

items.text: Early Nobatian houses at Qasr Ibrim had substantial stone walls, internal divisions and storage pits beneath floors. Straight intersecting lanes organised the settlement. The pits preserve evidence of keeping provisions within buildings.
Later houses at Qasr Ibrim used smaller stones, mud-brick partitions and compacted-earth floors. Some retained sunken storage bins. Building techniques changed while household storage continued.

A wooden game board found beside Tomb 3 at Qustul had ivory playing squares and silver fittings. A leather bag underneath contained fifteen ivory counters, fifteen ebony counters and five ivory dice. Researchers identify the game as Duodecim scripta, a relative of later backgammon. This late-antique royal burial find shows a well-equipped player’s world, although it cannot tell us who won or how widely families played.

The same Qustul set included fragments of a wooden dice tower with silver fittings and carved dolphins beside its lower opening. The reconstructed object shows the care put into gaming equipment as well as the board itself. Even the dice had a grand entrance. The surviving pieces do not preserve a complete local rulebook.

The great burial mounds at Qustul and Ballana cover elaborate underground tombs. Rich objects and the remains of sacrificed animals and people accompanied elite burials. They reveal concentrated power and coercion, rather than the living conditions of an average family.

Greek texts identify the kingdom as Noubadia and name Silko among its rulers. This written evidence helps connect political names with an archaeological landscape. The older label “X-Group” describes a research classification, not the people’s own name.

sections.title: Cloth in daily use and burial

items.text: At Qasr Ibrim, seams and hems allow researchers to distinguish some garments from otherwise unidentifiable scraps. Early medieval cotton also survives in cushions and reused rags used as mattress filling. Cloth could pass through several uses before entering the archaeological record.

Early Christian graves at Kulubnarti contain unusually open cotton fabrics interpreted as shrouds. Other funerary bindings combine light plant fibres with dark wool. These finds show choices in fibre, structure and colour, but burial cloth cannot stand for an entire everyday wardrobe.

The early seventh-century church at Faras was followed by a later cathedral. Surviving wall paintings were applied in tempera to plaster. Most of the preserved paintings date from the eighth to fourteenth centuries, after independent Nobatia.

Faras preserves epitaphs naming clergy and locally produced pottery alongside its painted walls. These are different kinds of evidence for a religious community: written remembrance, workshop production and decorated spaces used for worship.

In later medieval Nubia, painters of luxury pottery adapted motifs also found in manuscripts and church decoration. Some broken bowls were drilled and stitched together again. These repairs reveal the value attached to decorated vessels and the work invested in extending their use.

Medieval Nubian texts survive in Greek, Coptic and Old Nubian, sometimes combining languages. Religious fragments and commercial or legal documents preserve different uses of writing. This later record should not be projected unchanged into the earlier independent kingdom.

sections.title: People and their words in the later region

items.text: Two foundation texts at Faras, in Greek and Coptic, commemorate Bishop Paulos’s cathedral in 707. They name King Mercurius, linking the building to a Makurian ruler governing the northern region. These carved records help historians trace political change; the date of a cathedral’s foundation does not by itself date the kingdoms’ union.

A Faras visitor named Ogijino left a short invocation to Jesus with his name on a wall. His signature survives in the published record, but his occupation and reason for visiting are unknown. It preserves one person’s wish to be remembered in a religious place.

A twelfth-century Old Nubian list of church properties was found at Qasr Ibrim in a jar beneath a house floor. Its paper had been folded along four horizontal and three vertical lines. The document connects landholding with careful record keeping in the later Nobadian region. A pottery jar could hold paperwork as well as provisions.

A 2023 re-reading of a Faras church inscription identifies Iesousanya as a female deacon and the daughter of Marianos Osa. The text probably dates to the thirteenth or fourteenth century, long after independent Nobatia. The original plaster crumbled after excavation, so a tracing preserves the evidence. This interpretation recovers a woman’s religious role and family connection without establishing the duties or status of every woman.

sections.title: A familiar gesture, and paintings saved

items.text: A Faras painting of Saint Anne shows a finger touching her lips. The museum dates it broadly from the eighth to early tenth century. Curator Bożena Mierzejewska discusses silence and prayer as possible meanings of the gesture. It may look like a familiar request to be quiet, but its religious meaning needs its own explanation. The surviving image is fragmentary, so Anne’s original full pose is uncertain.

Faras’s cathedral was submerged in 1964, but paintings, inscriptions and other objects had been removed during rescue excavations. They preserved parts of the building’s history for study after the walls themselves became inaccessible. Conservation can save clues as well as beautiful pictures.

ending.text: Nobatia joined Makuria, but the timing remains debated. Proposed dates extend from the seventh century into the early eighth. This ended separate kingship while northern Nubian communities continued under changed institutions. The map’s 800 endpoint is a coverage boundary, not a verified conquest or disappearance of the population.
